explanations.explanation: God says, "I thought that after she had done all these things, she would return to Me." (Jeremiah 3:7) Hills, trees, the whole tour, and He still figured she'd come home. That's what He expected from her. Keep that in your pocket, friend, because the whole passage keeps coming back to this.
Not what God says here. He says what He thought she would do: "…she would return to Me." (Jeremiah 3:7) Nothing in this verse is about her packing up or moving out. It's about her coming back to Him.

Judah does show up in this verse, but only as the unfaithful sister who saw what happened (Jeremiah 3:7). God's thought is about Israel and Him: "…she would return to Me." Sister peace talks never come up. Nice thought, though, since families sure do need them.

God says, "I gave her a certificate of divorce and sent her away." (Jeremiah 3:8) It happened because faithless Israel had committed adultery. That's the paper in this verse. Nobody's going to frame it.
No real estate in this verse, baker. No moving truck either. What God gave her was "a certificate of divorce" before He sent her away (Jeremiah 3:8).
I love a fresh start, but there's no name change in this verse. What God says He gave was "a certificate of divorce." (Jeremiah 3:8) Then He sent her away. No hello-my-name-is sticker here.

I get why you'd think so, since you'd figure that would shake somebody up. But the text says Judah "had no fear and prostituted herself as well." (Jeremiah 3:8) She saw Israel sent away and went right on. So the answer here is False.

Right on. Judah watched Israel get sent away, and the text says she "had no fear and prostituted herself as well." (Jeremiah 3:8) She saw it all happen and kept going anyway. That's one stubborn sister.

God says Judah "did not return to Me with all her heart, but only in pretense." (Jeremiah 3:10) That's like a person who shows up to the kitchen in an apron and never touches the dough. The look was there. The heart wasn't, all the way.

Fear is the one thing the text says Judah didn't have. Earlier it says she "had no fear" and went right on prostituting herself (Jeremiah 3:8). When she did come back, it was "only in pretense." (Jeremiah 3:10)

Tears come later in this passage, when the children of Israel are heard weeping (Jeremiah 3:21). Here, in verse 10, the word is "pretense." Judah did not return "with all her heart, but only in pretense." No crying in this verse, friend.

Yes, ma'am, yes, sir, that's what it says. The LORD tells Jeremiah, "Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than unfaithful Judah." (Jeremiah 3:11) Read that again slowly. Israel, the one who got sent away, comes out looking better than Judah.

I know, I did a double take too. But the text says it plain: "Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than unfaithful Judah." (Jeremiah 3:11) Israel got sent away, and still she's the one ahead of Judah here. So the answer is True.

"I will no longer look on you with anger, for I am merciful." (Jeremiah 3:12) That's God's own reason, right there in His words. And He adds, "I will not be angry forever." Say that one out loud, baker.
Nothing in the text says God is satisfied. The reason He gives is His own character: "for I am merciful." (Jeremiah 3:12) That's the word to hold on to.

God doesn't say He's finished with her. He says, "I will no longer look on you with anger, for I am merciful." (Jeremiah 3:12) And in the very same breath He says, "Return, O faithless Israel." Does that sound like somebody who's finished?

God says, "Only acknowledge your guilt, that you have rebelled against the LORD your God." (Jeremiah 3:13) Notice that word "only." No receipt, no apology tour, just own it. Easier said than done, I know. I spent years in a drawer pretending I wasn't worn out.

No construction crew in this verse, baker. God asks for one thing: "Only acknowledge your guilt, that you have rebelled against the LORD your God." (Jeremiah 3:13) That's the ask. Keep your hammer in the toolbox.
No bill is handed over here. God says, "Only acknowledge your guilt, that you have rebelled against the LORD your God." (Jeremiah 3:13) That's the one thing He names. It's about owning the rebellion.

God says, "Then I will give you shepherds after My own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding." (Jeremiah 3:15) That's a different kind of meal, friend. These shepherds feed people what they need to know. And I love that He calls them shepherds after His own heart.

Gold and silver would look nice on a shelf, but they're not on the menu here. These shepherds "will feed you with knowledge and understanding." (Jeremiah 3:15) You can't bake with gold, anyway. I've tried to stamp it, and nothing.
Close in sound, but that's not what the verse says. The shepherds "will feed you with knowledge and understanding." (Jeremiah 3:15) And God calls them shepherds "after My own heart."

That's what God says: "It will never come to mind, and no one will remember it or miss it, nor will another one be made." (Jeremiah 3:16) He's talking about "those days," when they multiply and increase in the land. I'll leave it right at His words, and I won't guess past them.

God says the opposite of that. Of the ark He says, "It will never come to mind, and no one will remember it or miss it, nor will another one be made." (Jeremiah 3:16) That's how it goes in "those days." So the answer is True.

God says, "At that time they will call Jerusalem The Throne of the LORD, and all the nations will be gathered in Jerusalem to honor the name of the LORD." (Jeremiah 3:17) That's a new name for the city. And look at who's coming: all the nations.
That one sounds lovely, but it's not what God says. He says they will call Jerusalem "The Throne of the LORD." (Jeremiah 3:17) The nations gather there to honor His name.
Sounds like a vacation brochure, doesn't it? But the text says they will call Jerusalem "The Throne of the LORD." (Jeremiah 3:17) And the nations come to honor the name of the LORD.

God says, "They will no longer follow the stubbornness of their evil hearts." (Jeremiah 3:17) That's part of what He says about that time. It's a promise for the days ahead. The stubbornness stops following them around.
Look at the verse again. God says of that time, "They will no longer follow the stubbornness of their evil hearts." (Jeremiah 3:17) So that is exactly what He says. The answer is True.

"In those days the house of Judah will walk with the house of Israel, and they will come together from the land of the north." (Jeremiah 3:18) Remember those two unfaithful sisters? Now they're walking together. I'd pay good money to see that family reunion.
Egypt doesn't show up anywhere in this verse. The text says the house of Judah will walk "with the house of Israel." (Jeremiah 3:18) And they come together from the land of the north.
Edom isn't in this verse, friend. The text says the house of Judah "will walk with the house of Israel." (Jeremiah 3:18) Two houses, together, coming from the land of the north.

God says, "I thought you would call Me 'Father' and never turn away from following Me." (Jeremiah 3:19) That's what He had in mind for them. It comes right after He says He longs to make them His sons. Friend, I read that line and I sit down for a minute.

Good word, but it's not the one God uses. He says, "I thought you would call Me 'Father' and never turn away from following Me." (Jeremiah 3:19) It goes with what He said just before, that He longed to make them His sons.
Not this time. God says, "I thought you would call Me 'Father' and never turn away from following Me." (Jeremiah 3:19) It's a family word, and it fits with His wish to make them His sons.

explanations.answer: They had turned away and forgotten the LORD
explanations.explanation: The text says they are weeping and begging for mercy "because they have perverted their ways and forgotten the LORD their God." (Jeremiah 3:21) That's the reason it gives. A voice heard on the barren heights, and it's the sound of people who know it.

explanations.answer: Enemies had taken away all their land
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It gives the reason: "because they have perverted their ways and forgotten the LORD their God." (Jeremiah 3:21) That's what the weeping is about.

explanations.answer: Their king had been killed in battle
explanations.explanation: No king and no battle in this verse, baker. The weeping comes "because they have perverted their ways and forgotten the LORD their God." (Jeremiah 3:21) That's the only reason the text gives.
God says, "Return, O faithless children, and I will heal your faithlessness." (Jeremiah 3:22) Heal, friend. Not just point at it, but fix it. That's an invitation worth saying yes to.
That's not what God says here. His promise is, "I will heal your faithlessness." (Jeremiah 3:22) It comes right after He calls, "Return, O faithless children."
God doesn't say He'll look the other way. He says, "I will heal your faithlessness." (Jeremiah 3:22) That's more than overlooking it. It's something He does for them.

Almost, but flip it around. The people say, "Surely deception comes from the hills, and commotion from the mountains." (Jeremiah 3:23) Then they say where salvation is: "Surely the salvation of Israel is in the LORD our God." So the answer is False.

Right on. The people say deception comes from the hills and commotion from the mountains. Then comes the line that counts: "Surely the salvation of Israel is in the LORD our God." (Jeremiah 3:23) They finally know where to look.

The people say, "We have sinned against the LORD our God, both we and our fathers." (Jeremiah 3:25) Nobody points a finger at somebody else. They say we, and they say our fathers. That's owning it, baker.

That's not what they say. They say, "We have sinned against the LORD our God, both we and our fathers." (Jeremiah 3:25) The "we" is right there in the verse. They don't hand it all to the people before them.
No kings or priests get named here. The people say, "We have sinned against the LORD our God, both we and our fathers." (Jeremiah 3:25) They put themselves right in it.
They say it themselves: "from our youth even to this day we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God." (Jeremiah 3:25) No dodging and no excuses. I think that's hard to say out loud.
It's actually what the people say. Their words are, "from our youth even to this day we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God." (Jeremiah 3:25) So the answer is True.

God says, "If you will remove your detestable idols from My sight and no longer waver…" (Jeremiah 4:1) That's what has to go. And it begins with an "if," so it's an open door. Those idols are clutter, friend.
No weapons are mentioned here. God says, "If you will remove your detestable idols from My sight and no longer waver…" (Jeremiah 4:1) The idols are what He names.
No walls in this verse, baker. The thing God names is "your detestable idols." (Jeremiah 4:1) Those are what He says to remove from His sight.
God says, "…then the nations will be blessed by Him, and in Him they will glory." (Jeremiah 4:2) It's all of the nations, not just Israel. That's a big blessing hanging on a small word like "if."
Priests aren't named in this verse. God says, "…then the nations will be blessed by Him, and in Him they will glory." (Jeremiah 4:2) It reaches way past one group.
Elders don't show up here, friend. The verse says, "…then the nations will be blessed by Him, and in Him they will glory." (Jeremiah 4:2) That's a wide blessing.
God says, "Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and remove the foreskins of your hearts." (Jeremiah 4:4) It's the heart He names, the inside. Not just the outside, friend.
Hands aren't what He names. God says, "Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and remove the foreskins of your hearts." (Jeremiah 4:4) It's the hearts.
Eyes aren't in this verse. God says, "Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and remove the foreskins of your hearts." (Jeremiah 4:4) The word is hearts, baker.

I'd love for that to be so, but it's not what God says. He says, "My wrath will break out like fire and burn with no one to extinguish it, because of your evil deeds." (Jeremiah 4:4) That isn't a flash that passes. This one is heavy, so the answer is False.

Right. God says, "Otherwise, My wrath will break out like fire and burn with no one to extinguish it, because of your evil deeds." (Jeremiah 4:4) It doesn't flare and fade. I think it's a heavy verse, and it's a good reason to listen to that word return.
